summary:
Our game, Axo-nauts, puts you in the seat of the CEO of a major space program led by the cutest animals we know, axolotls! The possibilites range from exploring the Tona system, falling into a black hole, watching meteor showers above, appreciating the northern lights (aurora borealis) from above, mining resources and meeting other species on other planets, surviving dust-storms on Rusk and so much more! Its purpose it bring the knowledge of rocket science, key decision-making skills through crew decisions and managing different departments related to finances, resources, the availability of the crew, building the rocket, design review and purpose of a space centre to all ages around the world. For younger audiences or beginners, we've also added a dedicated "Simple Mode" for them to learn the ropes. When they are ready to move on, they can switch "Simple Mode" off and use elements such as the gimbal, SAS, RCS, orbital manouvers and manouvering the aircraft manually. By gamifying the entire learning process, it makes every step of the way educational (paired with the use of the Axo-Pedia) and fun! We hope you folks at NASA enjoy this one, we hope to see you soon and have a good one!

“We learn best in moments of enjoyment.” — Dr. Ralph C. Smedley
details:
Purpose

Axo-nauts is a space mission simulator that lets players experience the challenges of real space exploration, from solar storms and dust storms to eclipses and black holes. Instead of human astronauts, the crew is made up of axolotls who discover an abandoned space centre and set out to explore their solar system.

The game includes Career, Sandbox and Scenario modes, alongside a collection of mini-games. Each can be played in Simple Mode, which focuses on fun and ease of play, or Standard Mode, which offers detailed statistics, realistic orbital mechanics and full control over spacecraft design.

Impact

Axo-nauts teaches real physics through play. To reach orbit, players need to understand thrust-to-weight ratio, staging and why horizontal speed matters as much as altitude. Landing on a moon introduces gravity and delta-v, while descending through a thin atmosphere shows why parachutes behave differently on each world.

We designed the game to be accessible to as many people as possible. Graphics quality can be lowered for less powerful devices, and Simple Mode and step-by-step tutorials ensure beginners never get stuck, while Standard Mode still challenges experienced players. The crew system adds another layer: each axolotl has a name, a mood and food and water needs, encouraging players to plan for life support and care about their crew, not just the rocket.

Ultimately, we want space science to feel welcoming to students who believe physics is "not for them." For many, orbital mechanics begins as equations on a whiteboard; we wanted it to begin with an axolotl cheering as their rocket finally reaches orbit. We hope players finish Axo-nauts understanding how a real launch works and eager to keep learning about space, engineering and coding.

Technical Information

Axo-nauts is built with JavaScript, HTML and CSS, and the entire game runs from a single HTML file. 3D graphics are rendered in WebGL using the three.js library, which is embedded in the file, so the game works offline without installation. We wrote custom GLSL shaders for effects such as bloom, lens flare and water, as well as our own physics engine, which models orbits, spheres of influence, atmospheric drag, staging and ground collisions. Sound is handled by the Web Audio API, and progress is saved locally in the browser.

Multiplayer supports up to four players through a Google Firebase Realtime Database, with a small Python server for local testing. The game was developed on a Windows laptop with help from Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant, and tested using automated scripts that played through missions in headless Chrome to catch bugs. It runs in any modern browser on a laptop, desktop or tablet.

Creative Aspects

Most realistic space games are serious and difficult to get into, so we paired real physics with a soft, pastel world. The axolotls' home planet, Xochi, is named after Xochimilco, the Mexican lake where wild axolotls live, and every world in the Tona system has its own personality. Lull's thick purple atmosphere makes it easy to land on but very hard to leave, while Cinder is "scorching, airless and sparkly."

The crew comes in real axolotl colour varieties, including leucistic, golden, wild type, melanoid and glowing GFP, alongside an alien species called the Glimmerkin. Story events present players with choices, such as discovering a stowaway, comforting a homesick crew member or making first contact with alien life. We also created our own mechanics: Simple Mode turns long journeys into an arcade-style dash through asteroid belts and storms, the black hole Gulp features a glowing accretion disk and tidal "spaghettification," and players can walk around inside their space habitats.

Considerations

People often debate whether the journey or the destination matters more, but we believe it is the company. That is why we included a multiplayer mode, where players work together to solve problems and sharpen their logical thinking while flying their axolotl crews around the Tona system.

Our biggest challenge was balancing realism with fun. We kept real physics for gravity, orbits, drag and fuel, since that is what makes the game educational. To keep it accessible, we made it free and browser-based, with touch controls, tutorials and a reduced-motion setting. Because many students use school laptops rather than gaming PCs, we load terrain in the background and keep visual effects light so the game runs smoothly. Every mission is built around a single real concept, such as reaching orbit or surviving a dust storm. Finally, as wild axolotls are critically endangered, we used their real colour varieties and a lake-inspired home world to spark curiosity about the species.
